A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MI-TUNE and retain matching algorithms, theory and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable in both versions, supporting a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original T2I-CompBench experiments, alignment-metric comparisons, human studies and fine-tuning ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds SDXL, DiffusionDB, image-quality evaluations and further diagnostic experiments.

M1.justification: The MI estimator and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same generation, MI-ranking, top-k selection and adapter fine-tuning procedure. v2 additionally defines model-combination variants through averaging category-specific DoRA weights and jointly training on category datasets (Appendix E.3).

E1.justification: T2I-CompBench and the CC12M mixing experiment are retained. v2 adds actual training and evaluation with human-written DiffusionDB prompts, previously only cited, and MS-COCO-2014 image-quality evaluation. These substantially broaden the evaluated data and prompt complexity.

E2.justification: The six original alignment competitors remain, but v2 expands HPS comparisons from category-selected competitors to all six. It adds HPS-selected fine-tuning and direct DiffusionDB-image fine-tuning comparators. Table 2 also compares image quality against DALL-E-3, Imagen-3 and SDXL using explicitly attributed published scores.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's fixed CFG=7.5 and separately reported fine-tuning rounds, v2 introduces joint round/CFG selection, SDXL experiments, and FID, FD-DINO and CMMD evaluation on 30,000 COCO samples. Spatial adaptation is now described as using SPRIGHT-generated training images rather than fine-tuning SPRIGHT itself. DiffusionDB introduces an HPS-only protocol, although Section 4.1 and Appendix H.1 give inconsistent split counts.

E4.justification: v2 adds alignment–quality sensitivity to guidance and fine-tuning rounds, HPS-versus-MI sample selection, category-model merging and joint training, rank-conditioned score distributions, and BLIP-VQA decomposition failure examples. Existing candidate-pool and adapter/CLIP ablations are retained in Appendix E rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix J adds empirical score-distribution estimation: MI-rank-conditioned CDFs for three metrics across 700 prompts and 50 images per prompt. This extends descriptive statistical reporting beyond v1's aggregate scores and Kendall correlations. Neither version supplies repeated-run error bars, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds image-quality, SDXL, DiffusionDB and model-combination results. Its main MI-TUNE row changes under revised round/CFG selection, including Color 61.57 to 65.04 and Texture 58.27 to 65.82; these represent different reported settings. Human-study Texture changes from 51.2 to 53.19 beyond rounding, reversing its ranking against A&E (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 7), without an explained survey expansion.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(2), the diffusion-process definitions, the perfect-training assumption and the Appendix A derivation are mathematically unchanged. Added metric explanations and empirical distributions introduce no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v1 claims competitive performance and superiority on most alignment categories. v2 claims superiority across all explored categories and metrics, explicitly claims the first fully self-supervised approach, and adds SDXL/realistic-prompt generalization and balancing alignment with image quality to its stated contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains alignment–quality trade-offs and CFG mitigation, category conflicts, evaluation-metric selection bias and BLIP-VQA's difficulty with complex prompts. Real-image mixing is reinterpreted as potentially helping aesthetics while reducing alignment. Conversely, v1's discussions of unreliable unconditional-denoiser MI estimates, unsuccessful alternative approaches and reduced interpretability disappear; dependence on the source model's alignment capability remains.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the UNet layers receiving DoRA, discloses five participants for the retained 42-survey method comparison, and adds batching, memory, per-prompt timing, DiffusionDB construction and spaCy-processing details. The Appendix C optimizer, adapter rank, training budget and hardware settings remain unchanged. These are principally additional disclosures.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting image-quality evaluation and recent alignment research, including CMMD, Comat, RealCompo and ConceptMix, while removing Lin and Yang's perceptual-loss reference. It sharpens the first-fully-self-supervised positioning and comparison with GORS. The central diffusion and MI research foundations remain the same.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, alignment-metric discussion and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Benchmark descriptions precede competing methods in v2; the standalone Discussion and concluding Limitations/Broader impact passages disappear. Appendices are substantially reorganized with more descriptive headings and cross-references.

P2.justification: v2 combines alignment, HPS and human-study results into a redesigned Table 1 with averages and gain heatmaps. It places algorithms side by side and adds quality, sensitivity, model-merging and score-distribution displays, plus SDXL and DiffusionDB image grids. Existing qualitative grids are reformatted and shortened.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps by measuring the image-quality cost of alignment and investigating CFG mitigation (Figure 2, Table 2), testing SDXL and realistic DiffusionDB prompts, and adding selection and model-combination diagnostics. These substantially strengthen evidence about generality and practical trade-offs. Dropped estimator limitations, unexplained human-score changes and conflicting DiffusionDB counts reduce transparency, but the added validation still provides a substantial net improvement.
